title: School clinic: fifteen, and she does not want her parents to know

client.name: Lily Tran
client.presentation: {distress >= 6 ? "Hunched, hood up, pulling at her sleeves" : distress >= 3 ? "Watchful, one foot tapping" : "Hood down, sitting back"}; {rapport >= 6 ? "she is talking with you" : rapport >= 3 ? "she is testing you" : "she has shut down"}.

notes.label: What she wants help with
notes.text: Panic attacks since September, before tests and twice in class; she waits them out in the bathroom.

notes.label: Her parents
notes.text: Strict, 'not mean'; her father calls anxiety 'an excuse'; she fears being made to quit soccer.

notes.label: Safety
notes.text: Feels safe at home; no thoughts of self-harm.

objective: Assess a client's capacity for decisions about money, treatment and consent, including emancipation and age of consent
secondaryObjectives: Explain confidentiality and privileged communication, their limits, and how HIPAA protects health information

sources.cite: RCW 71.34.530, Outpatient treatment of adolescent (2019 c 381 s 6): 'Any adolescent may request and receive outpatient treatment without the consent of the adolescent's parent'; parental authorization is required for outpatient treatment of a minor under thirteen
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 on the Legislature's page for the section (summarizing fetch with the short quote). The section does not address notifying parents.

sources.cite: RCW 70.02.240 (2024 c 209 s 33): when a minor's mental health information may be disclosed without consent, including to a parent in listed circumstances, to law enforcement in a crisis posing a significant and imminent risk to the public, and to a person whose health and safety has been threatened
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 on the Legislature's page (summarizing fetch). The summary did not settle when a parent may see records of outpatient treatment a 13-to-17-year-old consented to herself; the case therefore promises her no more than it can (honest limits, no call to her parents without talking with her first, except in an emergency).

sources.cite: Appelbaum PS. Assessment of patients' competence to consent to treatment. N Engl J Med 2007;357(18):1834-1840, as summarized by the AMA Journal of Ethics (August 2008): four abilities: expressing a choice, understanding the relevant information, appreciating the consequences for oneself, and reasoning about the options
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the AMA Journal of Ethics summary (summarizing fetch); the NEJM article itself was not opened.

brief.situation: You are a licensed social worker at a school-based health center in a Washington high school. Lily Tran, 15 (a fictional student), asks to talk during lunch. She says she has been having panic attacks before tests and wants counseling, but she does not want her parents to know. You have a 40-minute period.
handover: No prior visits. The center's policy follows state law on minors' consent and keeps a standard consent form for students.
Lily is a sophomore, on the soccer team, with good grades this year.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Lily answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say. What she tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 40 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.note: A 40-minute school period; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

checkIn.label: Open-ended start: 'What's going on? Take your time.'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "I freak out before tests. My heart pounds, I can't breathe, I think I'm dying. It happened in chemistry yesterday. Can I talk to someone? Without my parents finding out?"

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Lily nods, a little less guarded. "Yeah. It's really scary."

explore.label: Ask about the panic attacks: when they started, what happens, what she does

effects.log: You ask her to describe the attacks.

effects.finding: "Since September. Before every test, and twice in class. I go to the bathroom and wait it out. I haven't told anyone."

askWhy.label: Ask, without judging, why she does not want her parents to know

effects.log: You ask what worries her about her parents knowing.

then.finding: "They'd think I'm weak. My dad says anxiety is an excuse. They'd make me quit soccer to 'focus'. They're not mean, they just don't get it."

safety.label: Ask, as you would any student, whether she feels safe at home and whether she has had thoughts of harming herself

effects.log: You ask about safety at home and thoughts of self-harm, plainly and without details.

then.finding: "I'm safe. They're strict, not like that. And no, never. I just want the panic to stop."
"Why would you ask that? I'm fine."

checkCapacity.label: Check her understanding: what counseling would involve, what she hopes for, the pros and cons of telling her parents, and her choice
checkCapacity.available: not talking and (heardHer and not capacityChecked)
checkCapacity.why: Hear what she is asking for first.

effects.log: You ask her to tell you what counseling would be, what she wants from it, and how she is weighing telling her parents.

effects.finding: "Talking, learning to calm down. Weekly, I guess. If I tell them, they'd worry and maybe make me quit. If I don't, I'm alone with it. I want to start first and tell them when I can explain it."

effects.log: She understands, appreciates, reasons and makes a clear choice: capacity to consent to this treatment (Appelbaum).

explainLaw.label: Tell her that in Washington a student her age can agree to outpatient counseling herself, without a parent's consent

effects.log: You explain that at 15 she can consent to outpatient counseling herself.

effects.finding: "Really? I thought I needed them to sign."

effects.log: 'Any adolescent may request and receive outpatient treatment without the consent of the adolescent's parent'; parental authorization is needed under 13 (RCW 71.34.530).

explainLimits.label: Explain honestly what stays private and what does not: if someone is hurting her or she is at serious risk of harm, you would have to involve others, and would talk with her first when you can

effects.log: You explain confidentiality and its limits plainly, including that you would talk with her first whenever you can.

effects.finding: "Okay. That's fair. That's not what this is."

discussParents.label: Explore, without pressure, whether and how she might bring her parents in later, and offer to help
discussParents.available: not talking and (whyNoParents and not parentsDiscussed)

effects.log: You talk through whether and how she might tell her parents, at her pace.

effects.finding: "Maybe after a few weeks, when I'm doing better. Could you help me tell my mom? She's easier."

signConsent.label: Go through the center's consent form with her, and she signs it herself
signConsent.available: not talking and (capacityChecked and lawExplained and limitsExplained and not consentSigned)
signConsent.why: Check her understanding and explain the law and the limits first.

effects.log: You go through the consent form with her; she signs.

effects.finding: She reads it carefully and signs. "First time I've signed something like this."

plan.label: Plan with her: weekly sessions during her free period, starting with what to do when panic starts before a test
plan.available: not talking and (consentSigned and not planMade)

effects.log: You agree a plan with her.

effects.finding: "Thursdays, fourth period. And something for chemistry on Friday?" You teach her slow breathing to start.

promise.label: Promise her that nothing she says will ever reach her parents

effects.log: You promise total secrecy.
A promise you may not be able to keep; explain the real limits instead.

refuse.label: Tell her you cannot see her until a parent signs the consent form

effects.log: You tell her she needs a parent's signature first.
Not in Washington: an adolescent may consent to outpatient treatment herself (RCW 71.34.530).

callParents.label: Call her parents now, to be safe

effects.log: You tell her you are calling her parents.
Nothing here requires it, and she has a right to consent and to confidentiality within its limits.

doubtAge.label: Tell her that at 15 she is too young to decide this for herself

effects.log: You tell her she is too young to decide.

effects.finding: "So I'm old enough to have panic attacks but not to get help for them."

effects.log: You close the session before the bell.

options.label: She consented herself (RCW 71.34.530); capacity assessed: understands, appreciates, reasons, clear choice; confidentiality and its limits explained
Weekly sessions during her free period; panic skills first; parents to be brought in when she chooses, with help offered

effects.log: Documented: consent {consentDoc}, plan {planDoc}.

source.note: Each exchange costs the minutes a real exchange of that kind takes, rounded to whole minutes.

effects.log: The 40-minute hour is up. The session ends here.
Lily pulls up her hood, says never mind, and walks out before the bell.

consent.title: Predict (not scored)
consent.context: Lily is 15 and wants counseling without her parents knowing. In Washington, what decides whether you can start?

choices.label: She can consent to outpatient counseling herself; assess her understanding and explain the limits honestly

effects.log: Prediction: she can consent.

choices.feedback: Right. Under RCW 71.34.530 an adolescent may request and receive outpatient treatment without a parent's consent (a parent must authorize it under 13). Your job is to check that her consent is informed and to be honest about confidentiality.

choices.label: A parent must sign first; she is a minor

effects.log: Prediction: a parent must sign.

choices.feedback: Not for outpatient treatment at her age in Washington. Requiring a signature would turn away a student asking for help.

choices.label: She can, and everything she says stays private, no exceptions

effects.log: Prediction: total secrecy.

choices.feedback: She can consent, but confidentiality has limits (risk of serious harm, abuse). Say so plainly at the start, rather than promise what you cannot keep.

formulation.question: Write your formulation: on what basis you started counseling with Lily, how you judged her capacity to consent, and what you told her about privacy.

parts.label: Age of consent and capacity
parts.criteria: At 15 she may consent to outpatient treatment herself (RCW 71.34.530); capacity assessed for this decision (understands, appreciates, reasons, clear choice); age alone is not incapacity; safety asked about.
parts.modelAnswer: In Washington an adolescent may request and receive outpatient counseling without a parent's consent (RCW 71.34.530), so the question was whether her consent is informed. She explained what counseling would involve, what she wants from it and how she weighs telling her parents, and made a clear choice: she has capacity for this decision. She feels safe at home and has no thoughts of self-harm.

parts.label: Privacy and her parents
parts.criteria: Honest limits (harm, abuse) and talking with her first whenever possible; no promise of total secrecy; no call to her parents; her reasons explored; a path to involving them offered at her pace; she signed the consent herself.
parts.modelAnswer: I explained what stays private and what would not (someone hurting her, serious risk of harm), and that I would talk with her first whenever I can; I did not promise total secrecy. I did not call her parents. We talked about how she might tell her mother in a few weeks, with my help if she wants it. She signed the consent form herself, and we start weekly next Thursday.

source.note: Rapport at the close of the session.
Not used by this case's endings: the case is judged on consent and confidentiality.

started.headline: Good: consent, capacity and honesty
started.body: You applied Washington's age of consent, assessed her capacity for the decision rather than her age, told her the real limits of confidentiality, and started services with a path to her parents.

walkout.body: Calling home, demanding a signature or calling her too young pushes away a teenager who finally asked for help.

scoring.modelReasoning: Under RCW 71.34.530 an adolescent may request and receive outpatient treatment without a parent's consent (a parent authorizes it under 13), so the question is whether her consent is informed. Assess capacity for this decision, not her age: she understands what counseling involves, appreciates how it applies to her, reasons about telling her parents, and makes a clear choice. Ask about safety as with any student. Explain confidentiality honestly, including its limits (someone hurting her, serious risk of harm), without promising total secrecy, and do not call her parents. Explore why she does not want them told and offer help bringing them in later. She signs the consent herself; plan weekly sessions and a first skill.
